papers.title: BTBD9-driven IMPDH2 ubiquitination governs sleep homeostasis by gating adenosine metabolism in the basal forebrain.
papers.abstract: BTB domain containing 9 (BTBD9) is among the most reproducible genetic risk factors for sleep-related disorders, yet its molecular function in sleep regulation remains unclear. Here, we aimed to define the downstream substrate, core brain region, and molecular mechanism through which BTBD9 regulates sleep-wake homeostasis. Population-scale genomic and brain expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) datasets were integrated to infer the direction of BTBD9-associated genetic risk in sleep-related traits. Basal forebrain-specific neuronal manipulation of Btbd9 was combined with electroencephalography/electromyography (EEG/EMG)-based sleep analysis and fiberphotomerty to define the relevant brain locus and functional output. Ubiquitinomics, protein interaction, ubiquitination, and enzymatic assays were used to identify BTBD9-regulated substrates and determine how BTBD9-dependent modification affects metabolic enzyme activity. Basal forebrain-specific genetic disruption, receptor pharmacology, and adeno-associated virus (AAV)-delivered interfering peptides were further applied to test pathway necessity and reversibility in vivo. human genetic analyses showed that BTBD9 variants associated with higher expression predicted a pro-arousal tendency. Consistently, neuron-specific deletion of Btbd9 in the mouse basal forebrain increased non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and extracellular adenosine levels. Mechanistically, IMPDH2, the rate-limiting enzyme in de novo purine biosynthesis, was identified as a substrate of the Cullin-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase 3 (CRL3)BTBD9 ubiquitin ligase. BTBD9-mediated ubiquitination at IMPDH2 lysine 195 (K195) relieved guanosine triphosphate (GTP)-dependent allosteric inhibition, thereby limiting adenosine accumulation and sleep pressure. Basal forebrain neuronal knockout of Impdh2 recapitulated the sleep-promoting effect of Btbd9 deletion, whereas adenosine A1 receptor (A1R) blockade attenuated this phenotype. AAV-delivered interfering peptides targeting the BTBD9-IMPDH2 interaction reduced IMPDH2 ubiquitination, elevated adenosine levels, increased NREM sleep, and rescued BTBD9 overexpression-induced abnormal wakefulness in vivo. These findings identify a BTBD9-IMPDH2-adenosine pathway that links human genetic risk to basal forebrain control of sleep homeostasis. By defining BTBD9 as a molecular regulator of purine metabolism, this study provides a mechanistic framework for understanding and potentially targeting BTBD9-related sleep dysregulation.

papers.title: Distinct whole-brain c-Fos expression mapping following acute and chronic partial sleep deprivation in mice.
papers.abstract: Sleep loss constitutes a major health challenge, encompassing both acute sleep deprivation (ASD) and chronic partial sleep deprivation (CPSD). However, the differential impact of ASD and CPSD on brain-wide neuronal activity remains poorly understood. Here, we employed high-definition fluorescent micro-optical sectioning tomography (HD-fMOST) coupled with automated c-Fos quantification to systematically map global c-Fos expression in mice subjected to ASD, post-ASD recovery sleep (ASR), and CPSD. We found that 6 h of ASD broadly upregulated c-Fos expression, which was largely restored by 2 h of ASR. In contrast, 2 wk. of CPSD predominantly suppressed c-Fos but induced complex regional disparities. Cluster analysis delineated distinct activation patterns at the brain network level, whereas across conditions, similar trends were commonly observed in regions subserving related physiological functions. These findings reveal distinct whole-brain neuronal activation profiles following acute versus chronic sleep loss, highlighting potential neuromodulatory targets for treating sleep deprivation-induced dysfunction.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Acoustic Stimulation of Slow Oscillations Using a Wireless EEG Headband: A Polysomnography-Validated Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Acoustic stimulation precisely timed during sleep can enhance slow oscillations (SOs), a hallmark of deep sleep that is critical for restorative sleep. To date, this approach has largely been restricted to laboratory settings using high-density electroencephalography (EEG). Wearable EEG systems featuring closed-loop acoustic stimulation could enable scalable, home-based approaches to modulating slow-wave sleep. Here, we tested whether a real-time modeling approach (M-CLNS) could be implemented using a wireless EEG headband with forehead electrodes in healthy participants. Acoustic stimulation was delivered during a single night of sleep in alternating stimulation and sham conditions. We evaluated the accuracy of SO phase targeting utilizing the EEG headband and assessed whether it could be used to detect stimulation-induced changes in oscillatory dynamics. The findings were validated against simultaneous polysomnographic (PSG) recordings as an independent reference. We found that SO phase was targeted consistently near the intended phase using the headband, despite reduced amplitude and signal quality compared with simultaneous PSG. Acoustic stimulation produced an immediate enhancement of SO dynamics, as well as sustained increases in SO density and power spectral density within the SO and delta frequency range (0.75-5 Hz) during deep sleep. These effects were apparent both in the EEG headband and PSG signals. These results demonstrate the feasibility of closed-loop acoustic stimulation using a wireless EEG headband, providing a foundation for future home-based and clinical applications.

papers.title: Sleep and Drowsiness in Cattle: A Narrative Review of Physiology, Measurement, and Methodological Challenges.
papers.abstract: Sleep in cattle is a complex physiological state comprising non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, while drowsing represents an intermediate vigilance state between wakefulness and sleep. Research has progressed from invasive electrophysiological recordings to noninvasive polysomnography (PSG), behavioral assessment, accelerometry, and automated classification approaches. However, accurately identifying and quantifying vigilance states under production conditions remains challenging. This narrative review, based on 22 primary studies identified through searches of Web of Science, Scopus and Google Scholar, critically synthesizes current knowledge of sleep physiology in cattle, the approaches used to assess it, and the principal methodological limitations affecting interpretation of the available evidence. Cattle exhibit a polyphasic sleep pattern, with NREM generally accounting for the largest proportion of total sleep. However, reported sleep and drowsing durations vary considerably among studies, and these differences may reflect both biological variation and methodological factors. Drowsing is particularly difficult to characterize because its behavioral and physiological features overlap with quiet wakefulness and light sleep. Rumination represents an additional challenge because associated muscular activity can interfere with electrophysiological recordings and complicate vigilance-state classification. Behavioral observations and accelerometry provide scalable measures of resting and sleep-like behavior but cannot independently establish physiological sleep, whereas PSG provides greater physiological resolution while remaining susceptible to artifacts and practical constraints. Current evidence is insufficient to establish causal relationships between sleep variation and cattle health, welfare, or productive performance. Future research should improve physiological classification during overlapping behavioral states, better validate scalable monitoring approaches, and evaluate the functional consequences of sleep variation across diverse cattle populations and production conditions.

papers.title: A Unified Flexible Large Polysomnography Model for Sleep Staging and Downstream Clinical Screening
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is central to sleep medicine, yet its analysis remains hindered by labor-intensive manual scoring and limited cross-center generalizability. We present LPSGM, a large-scale PSG model trained on 220,500 hours of data from 16 public datasets (24,000 recordings) that addresses two challenges: cross-center sleep staging generalization and PSG-based screening of narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and depression. LPSGM integrates domain-adaptive pre-training, flexible channel configurations, and a unified architecture to accommodate heterogeneous recording protocols. In prospective validation, LPSGM achieves expert-level sleep staging ({kappa} = 0.845 {+/-} 0.066 vs. inter-expert {kappa} = 0.850 {+/-} 0.102) and matches fully supervised models on independent private cohorts. For downstream screening, LPSGM achieves 84.2% accuracy ({kappa} = 0.761) in three-class narcolepsy classification, with cross-institutional transfer for normal-versus-abnormal hypersomnia yielding an AUC of 0.879. Severe OSA screening reaches an AUC of 0.874 without access to respiratory signals. Depression symptom screening achieves an AUC of 0.801 in a surrogate-labeled APPLES cohort, and cross-dataset transfer to an independent clinically diagnosed cohort reaches an AUC of 0.965. These results suggest that LPSGM's pre-trained representations capture sleep-related signatures that generalize across institutions and support PSG-based screening of clinically relevant conditions. The code and pre-trained model are publicly available at https://github.com/Deng-GuiFeng/LPSGM.

papers.title: Sleep-dependent DNA methylation remodeling in basolateral amygdala fear engrams.
papers.abstract: How sleep consolidates fear memories at the molecular level within individual engram neurons is unknown. Using activity-dependent tagging and sequencing, we profiled the DNA methylome and transcriptome of engram and non-engram nuclei from the basolateral amygdala (BLA) after contextual fear conditioning with and without post-learning sleep deprivation. Fear learning induces coordinated CpG and CpH DNA methylation remodeling specifically in engram neurons, with each showing unique temporal dynamics, revealing CpH methylation as a separate component of the engram's epigenetic signature. Interestingly, sleep deprivation partially reverses learning-induced methylation changes and impairs memory recall, indicating that sleep supports engram-specific epigenetic consolidation. Integrating the engram methylome with single-cell transcriptome profiling, we construct a multi-omic molecular atlas of the BLA fear engram and identify Mid1 as a learning- and sleep-regulated methylation target. BLA-wide and engram-specific Mid1 knockdown establishes its functional requirement for fear memory consolidation, providing an approach to identify behaviorally relevant epigenetic targets.

Multi-omic integration identified Mid1 as a learning- and sleep-regulated methylation target whose BLA-wide and engram-specific knockdown impaired fear memory consolidation.

papers.title: A Physiology-Informed Deep Learning Approach for Sleep-EEG Brain Age Estimation.
papers.abstract: Sleep electroencephalography (EEG) contains rich signatures of biological aging, but deep-learning brain-age models often provide limited physiologic readouts. This study presents a physiology-informed deep learning framework that estimates brain age from whole-night polysomnography (PSG) and provides spectral-band-level and sleep-stage-level readouts of the features associated with age predictions. Trained and evaluated on approximately 10,000 PSG recordings across four cohorts (SHHS, MrOS, STAGES, and CFS), the model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 5.89 $\pm$ 5.01 years. External validation in an independent cohort (HomePAP) yielded an MAE of 5.41 $\pm$ 4.57 years. The brain age gap (BAG; predicted minus chronological age) was associated with mortality risk. Specifically, each 10-year increase in BAG was associated with a 19% increase in all-cause mortality risk (hazard ratio (HR)=1.19 [95% CI: 1.11-1.28]; p<0.001) and a 25% increase in cardiovascular mortality risk (HR=1.25 [1.07-1.46]; p=0.006) after adjustment for covariates. A trainable Gabor filter bank provides explicit center-frequency and bandwidth parameters for the learned spectral representation. Spectral features extracted using the learned filter bank explained additional variance in age beyond features computed from canonical EEG bands (incremental $\triangle \rm{R}^{2}$=4.7%; p<0.001). Attribution analysis with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) revealed age-dependent shifts in spectral importance, including decreased delta and increased beta contributions with age. The model also reflected known age-related changes in sleep stages (increased wake, reduced N3/REM). Collectively, these findings provide brain-age estimates with explicit spectral-band-level and sleep-stage-level readouts that align with established sleep neurophysiology.

papers.title: The role of BDNF, CREB, DAT, GFAP and Arc in manic- and OCD-like behavioral phenotypes in both sexes of rats exposed to REM sleep deprivation.
papers.abstract: Rapid-eye movement sleep deprivation (REM SD) has controversial effects on behavioral functions and cognitive abilities. Recent evidence has shown that REM SD in rats may lead to manic- and obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD)-like behaviors. The present study aimed to assess the effect of REM SD in both sexes of rats on locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, stereotyped behaviors, and OCD-like behavior. The possible role of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), cAMP response element-binding (CREB), dopamine transporter (DAT), glia fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and activity-regulated cytoskeleton-associated protein (Arc) was also assessed using real-time PCR. REM SD was done for 14 days (6 h/d). Locomotor activity, anxiety-like behavior, grooming, and sniffing were measured using the open field test, and the marble burying test measured repetitive/compulsive-like responses. The results showed REM SD in both sexes led to hyperlocomotion, decreased anxiety, and increased OCD-like and stereotyped behaviors, with more effects in females except anxiety-like behavior. Also, the expression level of BDNF, CREB, DAT, and Arc was decreased and GFAP was increased in the hippocampus of both sexes of REM SD rats, with more effects in females except CREB. In conclusion, and for the first time, the present study showed the possible role of Arc, DAT, and GFAP in the induction of OCD- and manic-like behaviors and stereotyped behaviors in both sexes of rats. We also observed reduced BDNF and CREB expression in REM SD animals, suggesting a potential association between these molecular alterations and the behavioral changes induced by REM SD. Interventions targeting these molecular pathways could offer promising therapeutic strategies for REM SD-induced mood disorders.

papers.title: RefineSleepNet: Task-Driven Signal-Domain Transformation for EEG/EOG Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging relies on effective representation of physiological signals. Representative raw-signal sleep-staging encoders typically transform input waveforms while progressively compressing their temporal resolution within the same encoding path. However, explicit modality-specific, sample-aligned, and task-driven signal-domain transformation before epoch-level feature extraction remains comparatively underexplored. To investigate this design, we propose RefineSleepNet, an end-to-end sequence-to-sequence framework that explicitly separates these two stages. Separately parameterized Signal Refinement U-Net (SRU-Net) branches first transform EEG and EOG waveforms while preserving the original temporal length, after which Epoch Feature Extractors (EFEs) extract epoch-level representations from the refined signals. Fused Sequence Attention (FSA) then performs multimodal integration and cross-epoch contextual modeling before epoch-wise classification. All stages are jointly optimized using the final sleep-staging objective without a separate waveform reconstruction target. RefineSleepNet was evaluated on Sleep-EDF-39, Sleep-EDF-153, and ISRUC-3 using subject-independent 10-fold cross-validation, achieving accuracy/macro-F1 (MF1) scores of 84.5%/79.8%, 83.5%/78.1%, and 80.3%/78.1%, respectively. Ablation experiments supported the coordinated design, while statistical analysis and intermediate-representation evaluations further examined the robustness and characteristics of the learned transformation. The learned transformation retained broad temporal and spectral organization while introducing local waveform changes and modality-specific spectral redistribution. These results support the staged organization as a viable modeling strategy for EEG/EOG sleep staging.

papers.title: CSPT-SleepNet: An Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Integrating Center-Driven Sequence Supervision and Multimodal Pyramid Token Encoding.
papers.abstract: Background: Automatic sleep staging is fundamental to sleep architecture analysis and the diagnosis of sleep disorders. Sleep staging requires jointly modeling complementary information across modalities, multi-scale physiological features, and temporal relationships across consecutive epochs. In target epoch prediction from consecutive epochs, non-target epochs primarily provide contextual information, but their ground-truth labels remain underused as auxiliary supervision. Methods: We propose CSPT-SleepNet, an automatic sleep staging framework integrating center-driven sequence supervision with multimodal pyramid token encoding. A Multimodal Pyramid Token Encoder extracts hierarchical multi-scale features from electroencephalogram, electrooculogram, and electromyogram signals, followed by intra-modal, cross-modal, and inter-epoch modeling for center-epoch classification. During training, the center epoch receives primary classification supervision, while non-center epochs receive weaker auxiliary supervision based on their ground-truth labels, providing stage-informed contextual support for the prediction target. Results: In subject-independent cross-validation on Sleep-EDF-20, Sleep-EDF-78, and ISRUC-S3, CSPT-SleepNet achieved accuracy (ACC)/macro F1 (MF1) scores of 87.93%/83.53%, 85.81%/80.87%, and 84.06%/82.86%, respectively. In a separate controlled comparison on Sleep-EDF-20, center-driven sequence supervision improved ACC and MF1 by 0.60 and 0.91 percentage points, respectively, over equal-weight sequence supervision. The full model has 3.418 million trainable parameters and requires 397.10 million floating-point operations for an input sequence of nine 30-s epochs. Conclusions: CSPT-SleepNet provides an effective framework for center-epoch sleep staging from consecutive multimodal inputs. Nevertheless, N1 recognition remains challenging, with F1 scores ranging from 55.3% to 62.7% across the three datasets.

papers.title: Daylight exposure improves sleep and subsequent sleepiness
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: The causal effects of daylight exposure on sleep remain poorly understood, particularly under real-world conditions. This study aimed to address this gap by examining the effects of an afternoon daylight intervention on subsequent sleep. Methods: Ten healthy participants (4 males; 19 to 28 years) completed two randomized 3-h afternoon outdoor walks under high-intensity light (HIL; clear goggles) or attenuated light (AL; neutral-density-filtered goggles; ~10 photopic lux) conditions. Light exposure was centered around the estimated crossover between the phase-advancing and phase-delaying portions of the light phase-response curve, individually determined from baseline dim light melatonin onset (DLMO). Subsequent nocturnal sleep was assessed using at-home polysomnography (PSG), and subjective sleepiness and sleep quality were assessed using the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale and Groningen Sleep Quality Scale, respectively. Differences between conditions and across time were examined using linear mixed-effects models. Results: There were no significant differences between conditions in DLMO timing or the phase angle between DLMO and sleep onset, indicating that the light manipulation did not produce a detectable shift in circadian phase. Sleep duration and self-reported sleep quality were also unchanged. However, nighttime delta power accumulated more rapidly following HIL exposure, accompanied by greater NREM sleep and reduced wakefulness after sleep onset (all p < 0.01). Participants were also significantly less sleepy upon awakening following HIL compared with AL exposure (p < 0.05). Conclusions: High-intensity natural daylight exposure may promote greater sleep intensity and reduce sleepiness upon awakening. These findings highlight a potential role for daytime light exposure in modulating subsequent sleep physiology and next-morning sleepiness, independent of changes in circadian phase.

papers.title: Postpartum mice display distinct behavioral and neuroimmune responses to chronic circadian disruption.
papers.abstract: The maternal brain undergoes profound adaptations during peripartum to support offspring development and maternal wellbeing. These adaptations are partly coordinated by neuroimmune signaling, including changes in the density and activity of microglia, the brain's resident immune cells. Microglia are regulated by the circadian system, which coordinates cellular activity across 24-h cycles, and disruption of circadian timing can alter neuroimmune activity and mood-related behaviors. Maternal rhythms are disrupted by offspring care demands; however, how such disruption affects maternal behavior, mood, and neuroimmune function remains unclear. We hypothesized that postpartum females would show greater behavioral and neuroimmune sensitivity to chronic circadian disruption than nulliparous controls. To test this, mice underwent a chronic phase advancement (CPA) paradigm (six-hour phase advance every four days) from postnatal days (P) 0-18 with behavioral testing occurring at an acute (P2-3) and chronic (P14-17) timepoint. Contrary to our prediction, maternal nest building and pup retrieval were maintained in mice after a single-phase shift. Sucrose preference was reduced by phase shifts at both the acute and chronic timepoint, but this reduction was comparable between parous and nulliparous females, showing no distinction based on parity. However, chronic CPA produced parity-dependent effects on behavior: CPA increased grooming and reduced nest preference in parous mice. In the medial preoptic area (MPOA), a brain region critical for maternal behavior, CPA reduced microglia density in parous compared to nulliparous females. MPOA transcriptomic analysis further showed parity × CPA interaction effects on synapse organization and RNA processing pathways. Chronic circadian disruption, therefore, shifts postpartum behavior, neuroimmune activity, and MPOA gene expression, in a distinct manner from nulliparous controls. Elucidating circadian-neuroimmune interactions in the postpartum brain may reveal novel targets for circadian-based interventions for postpartum mood disorders.

papers.title: MM-Net: A Multimodal Multi-Task Network for Sleep Staging and Sleep Apnea Assessment After Ischemic Stroke
papers.abstract: Automated polysomnography after ischemic stroke is challenging because of altered sleep-related neural activity and concurrent respiratory disturbances. Existing stroke-specific approaches mainly address sleep-stage classification, leaving joint analysis of sleep architecture and respiratory events underexplored. Moreover, adapting pretrained EEG encoders introduces a representation inconsistency when downstream models are trained on embeddings from previously seen patients but evaluated on unseen individuals. We propose MM-Net, a multimodal multi-task framework that resolves this inconsistency through cross-fitting and ridge-based embedding alignment. Sleep-adapted EEG-EOG representations and engineered neural descriptors are fused with learned cardiorespiratory features through cross-attention and shared temporal modeling for simultaneous sleep staging and respiratory-event detection. On iSLEEPS (99 patients with subacute ischemic stroke), ten-fold patient-independent evaluation achieved 76.3% staging accuracy (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.656) and 0.825 respiratory-event AUC, outperforming the evaluated baselines under matched protocols. The sleep-adapted encoder improved the downstream model when its embeddings were aligned, raising staging accuracy by 1.4 percentage points over the frozen encoder ($p$ = 0.020) versus 0.2 points without alignment. MM-Net also achieved 86.4% staging accuracy on Sleep-EDF, above every single-EEG architecture reimplemented on the same recordings, and 80.3% staging accuracy with 0.889 respiratory AUC on ISRUC-I, exceeding its retrained staging baselines. Without retraining, the iSLEEPS-trained model retained respiratory AUCs of 0.833 on ISRUC-I and 0.841 on UCD. These findings support representation-consistent neural adaptation and joint physiological modeling across stroke, healthy-sleep, and sleep-disorder cohorts.

papers.title: Ketones and Sleep: A Narrative Review of Mechanisms, Preclinical Models, and Human Evidence.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a metabolically dynamic state, and ketone bodies may interact with sleep physiology as both oxidative substrates and signaling metabolites. β-Hydroxybutyrate (BHB), acetoacetate (AcAc), and acetone rise during fasting, carbohydrate restriction, ketogenic diets used for therapeutic or non-therapeutic purposes, prolonged exercise, selected pathological states of insulin deficiency, and after consumption of exogenous ketones. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and human evidence linking endogenously generated ketosis and ketosis generated from exogenous ketone consumption to sleep architecture, sleep quality, sleep-disordered breathing, and sleep-relevant metabolic pathways. We reviewed studies involving ketogenic diets, fasting or caloric restriction, and consumption of exogenous ketones, prioritizing investigations with polysomnography, electroencephalography (EEG), sleep architecture, respiratory, or validated sleep-questionnaire outcomes, while also considering mechanistic studies of neuronal excitability, inflammation, epigenetic regulation, circadian timing, and brain energetics. The most direct preclinical evidence indicates that AcAc, but not BHB, increases slow-wave activity (delta power 0.5-4 Hz) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and suppresses glutamate release in mice, supporting a potential role for ketone metabolism in sleep homeostasis. Dietary, fasting, and aging models further suggest that lipid/ketone metabolism can alter NREM/rapid eye movement (REM) balance, circadian metabolic rhythms, and sleep-wake responses to energetic stress, with aged-rat data showing sex-specific REM and cognitive effects of ketogenic interventions. Human studies are suggestive but heterogeneous: acute carbohydrate restriction can increase slow-wave sleep and reduce REM sleep in healthy adults; ketogenic therapies may improve subjective sleep in selected neurological and metabolic populations; and ketone ester ingestion can improve sleep efficiency after strenuous evening exercise, but not during hypoxia-induced sleep disruption. Ketones are sleep-relevant metabolic signals, but their effects are conditional rather than universally sleep-promoting. They may also indirectly affect sleep by enhancing wakefulness quality. The ketone concentration range associated with optimal sleep outcomes remains undefined, and potential dose-, timing-, and context-dependent effects on sleep require further study. Future studies should distinguish AcAc from BHB biology, measure nocturnal ketone dynamics, incorporate PSG/EEG spectral endpoints, and separate ketosis-specific effects from weight loss, energy deficit, exercise load, respiratory physiology, circadian timing, and disease-related confounders.

papers.title: Indirect Skin Homeostasis Modulation by an Essential Oil Blend in Mice with Insomnia Comorbid Anxiety: Sensitivity of Dermal Fibroblasts to Exogenously Applied Circulating Molecules.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Studies have confirmed that essential oils extracted from aromatic plants exert mood-regulating and skin-beneficial effects. Although the concept of "emotional skincare" has attracted growing research interest, experimental evidence supporting the indirect skin-protective effects of essential oils through emotional regulation remains limited. This study investigates the indirect effect of an essential oil blend (EOB) on skin homeostasis in mice with insomnia comorbid anxiety (ICA, a pharmacologically validated emotional stress model induced by para-chlorophenylalanine) and aims to profile the sensitivity of dermal fibroblasts to candidate circulating molecules identified from EOB-treated ICA mice, thereby laying a mechanistic foundation for emotional skincare research. Methods: An essential oil blend (EOB) comprising lavender, Kushui rose, sweet orange, Roman chamomile, sandalwood, and clary sage essential oils was prepared. An ICA mouse model was established using para-chlorophenylalanine. Behavioral phenotypes, as well as neurotransmitter and hormonal indices, were measured to validate the anxiolytic and sleep disturbance-alleviating effects of EOB administered via intraperitoneal injection at 300 mg/kg per injection (two injections overall). Skin histological alterations and circulating biomarker profiles were evaluated, and selected differentially altered circulating molecules were exogenously applied to cultured dermal fibroblasts in vitro to assess their effects on fibroblast functions. Results: EOB significantly alleviated ICA-like behaviors and ameliorated abnormal levels of brain neurotransmitters and hormones in mice. Although only mild histological variations were observed in the skin after EOB intervention, significant alterations in cortisol, melatonin, 5-hydroxytryptamine, interleukin-10, and type I collagen were detected in serum or skin tissues. Exogenous application of these circulating molecules elicited differential responses in dermal fibroblasts, affecting oxidative stress, inflammatory responses, and extracellular matrix synthesis in a molecule-specific manner. Notably, these fibroblast assays only demonstrate cellular sensitivity in vitro and do not prove that these circulating molecules directly mediate the in vivo effects observed in mice. Conclusions: EOB intervention ameliorates insomnia- and anxiety-related behaviors and concurrent favorable changes in skin-associated molecular profiles in ICA mice. These changes are accompanied by alterations in circulating bioactive molecules to which dermal fibroblasts exhibit measurable sensitivity in vitro. These observations are consistent with, but do not definitively establish, a brain-skin axis-mediated mechanism. These findings provide preliminary experimental evidence for the emotional skincare concept and identify candidate circulating molecules for future causal validation; the in vivo regulatory roles of these molecules and the precise signaling pathways involved remain to be established in dedicated mechanistic studies.

papers.title: Effects of Circadian Phase and Exercise Training on Systemic and Tissue-Specific Redox Responses in Mice Fed a High-Fat Diet.

We investigated whether the circadian phase of training alters systemic and tissue-specific redox responses in HFD-fed mice. Male C57BL/6J mice fed an HFD remained sedentary or underwent 8 weeks of treadmill training at Zeitgeber time 3 (ZT3) or Zeitgeber time 15 (ZT15). Samples were collected 48 h after the final session. Plasma redox status was assessed using the OXY-adsorbent test (OXY), the derivatives of reactive oxygen metabolites test (d-ROMs; mainly reflecting circulating hydroperoxides), and the biological antioxidant potential test (BAP), and redox and inflammatory gene expression levels were quantified in three skeletal muscles and the liver. Exercise increased BAP (p = 0.0442), whereas OXY was unchanged. The phase × exercise interaction for d-ROMs showed a nonsignificant trend (p = 0.0560); exploratory comparisons showed higher d-ROMs in ZT15-sedentary (sed) than in ZT3-sed and ZT15-exercise (exe) mice. Gastrocnemius (GAS) Nfe2l2 showed a nominal phase × exercise interaction. Soleus (SOL) Hmox1 was higher at ZT15 and with exercise. Quadriceps (QUA) Nfe2l2 was higher at ZT3 and Cat at ZT15. Hepatic Keap1 was higher at ZT15, particularly in sedentary mice, while inflammatory transcripts remained largely unchanged. Only the phase effects on SOL Hmox1 and hepatic Keap1 remained significant after false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Long-term exercise was associated with higher plasma ferric-reducing capacity irrespective of circadian phase, whereas tissue redox-related transcriptional responses were mainly associated with circadian phase and differed among tissues. papers.title: Computational approaches to deep learning-driven EEG analysis for neurological disease diagnosis: a systematic review.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is a widely used non-invasive neurophysiological technique for analyzing brain dynamics and diagnosing neurological diseases. However, the non-stationary nature, low signal-to-noise ratio, and inter-subject variability of EEG signals cause significant challenges to traditional analytical approaches. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful computational tool for EEG analysis, which enables automated feature learning and improved diagnostic accuracy with minimal human-driven feature extraction. This review systematically explains computational approaches in deep learning-driven EEG analysis for the diagnosis of neurological diseases. It includes recent advances in deep learning architectures, such as convolutional neural networks (CNN), recurrent neural networks (RNN), hybrid configurations, Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN), Large Language Models (LLM), autoencoders, and transformer-based models, with a focus on their capacity to model spatial, temporal, and spatiotemporal dynamics in EEG signals. This is applicable in diagnosing major neurological disorders such as Epilepsy, Alzheimer's disease (AD), Encephalopathy, Parkinson's disease (PD), Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI), sleep disorders, and developmental brain disorders. Furthermore, we discuss essential preprocessing strategies and denoising techniques, showing how removing biological artifacts prevents diagnostic models from confusing noise with actual signs of disease. Key challenges such as limited data availability, lack of model interpretability, inter-subject variability, and difficulty in clinical translation are identified and critically discussed. Finally, key emerging trends and future research directions are identified to support the development of clinical applications of EEG-based disease diagnostic systems.

papers.title: Algorithmic loops and the developing brain: a narrative review of dopaminergic mechanisms, sleep disruption, and neuroplasticity.
papers.abstract: Generation Alpha (born ~2010-2024) is the first cohort whose critical windows of dopaminergic maturation overlap entirely with mass exposure to AI-optimised short-form looping video platforms. Despite a robust epidemiological signal linking social media to depression, anxiety, attention deficits, and sleep disruption in youth, direct causal neurobiological data remain absent. This narrative review synthesises evidence from developmental neuroscience, mesolimbic dopamine physiology, sleep medicine, and longitudinal neuroimaging cohorts to articulate a mechanistic framework: chronic exposure to algorithmically engineered variable ratio reinforcement schedules may produce homeostatic D2/D3 receptor downregulation in the developing striatum, functionally analogous to the neuroadaptations observed in substance use disorders. This deficit state, characterised by anhedonia and acquired attentional dysregulation, is plausibly amplified by algorithmic disruption of slow-wave sleep-the biological window for glymphatic metabolite clearance and synaptic homeostasis. Converging evidence from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study documents associations between screen behaviour and grey matter volume, reward-circuit activation, and executive function trajectories across early adolescence. Because direct in vivo measurement of D2 receptor density in children using PET radioligands is ethically prohibited, we propose a cross-species, multimodal longitudinal research framework. This integrates a novel nonhuman primate digital self-administration paradigm with human cohort studies utilising computational phenotyping of algorithmic dosage, polysomnographic sleep monitoring, and annual reward-task fMRI. Current evidence justifies both urgent regulatory action and a dedicated research programme to characterise the neurobiological consequences of a uniquely 21st-century exposure.

papers.title: A transient decrease in night-to-night variability of REM sleep before myocardial infarction
papers.abstract: Background. Myocardial infarction (MI) outcomes depend on time to treatment, and fatigue and sleep disturbance are often reported in the weeks before the event. Whether wearable-measured sleep changes within individuals before MI, and whether such change is specific to MI, is unknown. Methods. In the All of Us Research Program, adults with a first MI code and at least 180 valid Fitbit sleep nights in the preceding 360 days were matched to up to 10 controls on sex, comorbidities, sleep apnea, calendar time and a propensity score. The full matched cohort of all cases was the primary cohort, and cases with diabetes and/or hypertension formed a subgroup. The main endpoints were the within-person change in night-to-night variability (SD, RMSSD, CV) of the REM-sleep fraction at days 30-16 relative to each persons baseline (days 360-121) and from days 30-16 to days 15-1, tested against 10,000 randomly placed index dates with allowance for the choice of window (max-T). The same pipeline was applied to cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, to an index date at the first angina code, to a cohort including heart failure and to ischaemic stroke and admissions for heart failure, pneumonia, fracture or appendicitis and any cause, and the analysis was adjusted for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Results. The full matched cohort comprised 45 cases and 450 controls. REM-fraction variability changed transiently before MI, decreasing at days 30-16 and returning towards baseline over days 15-1; allowing for the choice of window, this decrease-then-return pattern was rarely matched at 10,000 randomly placed index dates (max-T p<0.001). Its components were the decrease in SD at days 30-16 (Cliffs {delta} -0.30, p=0.004; OR per SD 0.53, 95% CI 0.35-0.80; max-T p=0.0034) and the return in RMSSD over days 15-1 ({delta} +0.36, p<0.001; max-T p=0.0035); day by day, the decrease was not detected as a continuous change (cluster permutation test p=0.58). The decrease in SD was not seen at the same time before admissions for pneumonia (69 cases), fracture or appendicitis (130) or any cause (859) and was larger before MI than before each of them (difference in {delta} -0.25 to -0.34), whereas the rise over days 15-1 was shared with pneumonia; it was of similar size in the subgroup with diabetes and/or hypertension, in cases without recorded symptoms or treatment, with the index date at the first angina code, when people with heart failure were included and after adjustment for nightly heart rate, wear and device. Scoring each person against their own baseline discriminated cases from controls with AUCs of up to 0.66, probably an optimistic estimate because the decrease in RMSSD was attenuated in held-out halves of the matched sets. Conclusions. In adults who use consumer wearables, a first MI was preceded by a transient change in night-to-night REM-sleep variability, a decrease at days 30-16 and a return over the following two weeks. The decrease was not seen at the same time before other acute admissions, did not depend on recorded symptoms or treatment and was detectable against each persons own baseline with simple measures. The timing is an exploratory finding, to be confirmed in new cases.

papers.abstract: Arousal, the activation dimension of the valence-arousal circumplex, indexes alertness and engagement independently of pleasantness. We evaluated whether MediaPipe FaceLandmarker iris landmark distances from a tablet camera estimate electroencephalography (EEG)- and photoplethysmography (PPG)-derived arousal markers during naturalistic reading. Recordings from 48 participants yielded 43,923 thirty-second windows. Raw iris distances correlated with EEG alpha (r=+0.118) and theta (r=+0.076), but face scale explained 93% of their variance. After face-width normalisation, alpha remained associated (r=+0.076), whereas theta was not statistically significant. Further adjustment for ocular luminance and head pose rendered alpha nonsignificant (r=+0.021, p=0.33). Circular-shift testing identified alpha coupling in 11/48 participants under full control, versus 28/48 using uncorrected Pearson tests. Within-subject Ridge regression, with no raw sample shared between the training and test windows, yielded a nonsignificant group mean correlation (r=+0.078, p=0.07); 13/48 participants had individually significant prediction-reference associations (11 positive), fewer when the PPG term was restricted to filter-consistent beats. Both counts are exploratory, nominal and uncorrected across participants, and come from different analyses. Neither establishes prospective monitoring performance, and the study does not validate the landmark distance as a pupil measure.

papers.title: SOCS3 Suppression Is Associated with Hippocampal Inflammation in a Mouse Model of Intermittent Hypoxia.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Intermittent hypoxia (IH), a feature of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), is associated with hippocampal inflammation and cognitive dysfunction. We examined SOCS3 expression and a possible MALAT1/EZH2/H3K27me3 regulatory relationship in a mouse IH model and BV2 cells. Methods: C57BL/6J mice were exposed to IH for 4 weeks, followed by Morris water maze testing and analysis of hippocampal tissue. BV2 cells were exposed to IH and used for transfection, RNA immunoprecipitation, and chromatin immunoprecipitation experiments. Results: In mice, IH was associated with poorer water maze performance, lower hippocampal SOCS3, and higher levels of inflammatory markers, MALAT1, and H3K27me3. Similar molecular changes were observed in BV2 cells. SOCS3 overexpression reduced TRAF6, total NF-κB p65, TNF-α, and IL-1β protein levels in BV2 cells. MALAT1 was enriched by EZH2 immunoprecipitation, H3K27me3 was enriched at the SOCS3 promoter, and MALAT1 knockdown reduced total H3K27me3 while increasing SOCS3 protein. Conclusions: These findings associate reduced SOCS3 with hippocampal inflammation after IH and support further investigation of MALAT1 and EZH2 in its regulation. The cellular source of the in vivo inflammatory markers and the causal role of EZH2 require direct testing.

papers.title: Interventional Effects and Neurometabolic Regulation of a Panax quinquefolius-Containing Herbal Extract (JYF) in Diazepam Withdrawal Syndrome in Mice.
papers.abstract: Background: Long-term benzodiazepine use can lead to dependence and clinically significant withdrawal following discontinuation, highlighting the need to identify effective interventions for withdrawal-associated abnormalities. Methods: High-resolution mass spectrometry was used to characterize the constituents of a Panax quinquefolius-containing herbal extract (JYF) and evaluate their in vivo exposure in rats. Sixty-five C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to control, model, and low-, medium-, and high-dose JYF groups. Diazepam withdrawal was induced after 28 days of subcutaneous diazepam administration (12 mg/kg), and JYF was administered orally during the peri-withdrawal period for 7 days, beginning 4 days before diazepam discontinuation. Behavioral assessments, electroencephalographic/electromyographic (EEG/EMG) recordings, histopathological analysis, and neurochemical measurements were performed. Network proximity analysis, widely targeted metabolomics, targeted neurotransmitter quantification, and integrated pathway analysis were subsequently performed. Results: A total of 61 constituents were identified in JYF, of which 44 were detected in serum and 34 in brain tissue. Network proximity analysis highlighted genistein, columbamine, jatrorrhizine, and berberine as candidate constituents associated with withdrawal, anxiety/depression and sleep-related modules. JYF attenuated diazepam withdrawal-associated weight loss, anxiety-like behavior, sleep fragmentation, abnormal EEG activity, and elevations in corticosterone and orexin A. Metabolomic analyses revealed disturbances in lipid, energy, and amino acid metabolism, with tryptophan and phenylalanine metabolism emerging as prominent pathways associated with JYF intervention. Diazepam withdrawal also disrupted cerebral monoamine homeostasis, as reflected by increased serotonin and norepinephrine and decreased dopamine levels; these alterations generally shifted toward control levels after JYF intervention. Conclusions: JYF alleviates behavioral and sleep-related abnormalities associated with diazepam withdrawal. Its effects may be associated with alterations in brain metabolic homeostasis, including tryptophan- and phenylalanine-related metabolism and monoaminergic neurotransmission. Genistein and berberine were identified as candidate active constituents that warrant further experimental validation.

papers.title: Association of Total Atherosclerosis Burden of Baroreceptor-Resident Arteries with Heart Rate Variability and Its Circadian Rhythm in Patients with Ischemic Stroke.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Post-stroke cardiac autonomic dysfunction is associated with poor neurological recovery and cardiovascular events. However, its association with vascular disease remains incompletely understood. We evaluated associations of atherosclerotic burden in baroreceptor-resident arteries (BRAs), including the carotid sinus (CS) and aortic arch (AA), with heart rate variability (HRV) and its circadian rhythm after ischemic stroke. Methods: This cross-sectional study consecutively enrolled 253 patients with first-ever ischemic stroke within 30 days of onset. Total atherosclerosis burden of baroreceptor-resident arteries (TAB-BRA) was assessed using computed tomography angiography (CTA), and patients were categorized based on TAB-BRA tertiles. The 24 h HRV indices and serial measures across 48 consecutive 30 min segments were derived from Holter recordings, with the standard deviation of all normal-to-normal intervals (SDNN) as the primary outcome. Results: After adjusting for age, sex, hypertension, stroke severity, time from stroke onset to Holter monitoring, and other prespecified covariates, each 1-point increase in TAB-BRA was associated with a 1.67 ms decrease in 24 h SDNN (95% confidence interval [CI], -2.43 to -0.90; p < 0.001), suggesting impaired cardiac autonomic regulation. Restricted cubic spline models revealed a nonlinear association (p for nonlinearity = 0.014). Adding AA burden to the model containing CS burden improved model fit for 24 h SDNN (adjusted R2 difference = 0.033; p = 0.001). Compared with Tertile 1, circadian SDNN amplitude was lower by 3.61 ms in Tertile 2 (95% CI, -6.33 to -0.81; p = 0.006) and 3.71 ms in Tertile 3 (95% CI, -6.59 to -0.77; p = 0.012). Conclusions: Higher TAB-BRA was nonlinearly associated with lower 24 h SDNN, while the intermediate- and high-burden groups had lower circadian SDNN amplitudes. papers.title: Editorial: Supporting the mental health of neurodivergent adults through sleep and circadian based interventions.
papers.abstract: Autistic, ADHD and AuDHD adults frequently experience sleep/circadian disruptions that impact their mental health. There is, however, a lack of effective and scalable interventions tailored for these groups that can address their treatment needs in this area. In this editorial, we summarise the challenge and propose a programme of basic science research that can inform the development of suitable interventions. We emphasise the importance of a co-design approach and of combining objective and subjective sleep/circadian measurement with mental health symptom data longitudinally to illuminate the within-person relations between sleep/circadian function and mental health. We highlight the need to better understand the sleep/circadian profiles of AuDHD individuals and their implications for mental health as a particularly critical gap.

papers.title: Using High-Performance Liquid Chromatography to Study Alterations in Biogenic Amines in Drosophila Models of Brain Disorders.
papers.abstract: Many neuropsychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders are characterized by disruptions in brain neurotransmitters, including alterations in the levels of the biogenic amines (BAs) dopamine (DA) and serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine; 5-HT), as well as in their release or reuptake. These neurochemical changes correlate with distinct key behavioral phenotypes, such as locomotor deficits, sleep fragmentation, and altered stress responses, among others. Because the principal BA systems interact, disease models frequently show coordinated shifts across multiple amines rather than isolated changes in a single neurotransmitter. Therefore, accurate, simultaneous quantification of several BAs is essential for interpreting behavioral and genetic findings. Drosophila melanogaster offers a genetically tractable system for modeling such disorders and neurotransmitter changes, but BAs occur in fly brain tissue at very low, nanomolar-to-femtomolar concentrations, and the small size of the Drosophila central nervous system makes their detection technically challenging. This study describes a protocol to detect and quantify DA, 5-HT, and octopamine in fly brains using high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with electrochemical detection (HPLC-ECD). HPLC-ECD was applied to detect changes in brain DA and 5-HT in a fly model of Parkinson's disease based on dopaminergic overexpression of human alpha-synuclein. Applying this protocol to the alpha-synuclein Parkinson's disease model reveals significantly elevated dopamine, but unchanged serotonin, relative to controls, consistent with early compensatory dopaminergic mechanisms. This approach provides a sensitive, low-cost, and readily accessible method for multiplexed BA quantification from limited Drosophila tissue. It also enables systematic screening of genetic modifiers and candidate therapeutics targeting monoaminergic pathways relevant to human brain disorders.

papers.title: Normative Deviation Modeling for EEG-based Depression Detection
papers.abstract: Web-enabled digital health services are expanding access to physiological monitoring and mental health screening. However, electroencephalography (EEG)-based major depressive disorder (MDD) detection remains challenging across heterogeneous data sources, where individual variability and acquisition differences may affect disease-related representations. In this work, we investigate the use of healthy normative references for EEG-based MDD detection. Specifically, structural and distributional reference models are independently trained using healthy control (HC) recordings to characterize departures from healthy EEG patterns. We develop two diagnostic approaches that incorporate normative deviations at different representation levels. Scalar-level Normative Deviation-guided Diagnosis (S-NDD) summarizes structural and distributional deviations into scalar scores and integrates them with deep EEG representations. Feature-level Normative Deviation-guided Diagnosis (F-NDD) retains dimension-wise residuals and combines them with deep EEG representations through attention-based aggregation and auxiliary supervision. We also employ target HC-assisted score calibration for cross-source evaluation without updating the trained models. Experiments on two public EEG datasets examine both approaches under subject-independent within-source and bidirectional cross-source settings. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of normative deviation-guided diagnosis across different evaluation settings.

Demographic files included 32 patients with MS and 32 healthy controls (HC); global-feature models included 29 patients with MS and 32 HC, and channel-level sample sizes varied by feature. Diagnosis and age were entered in linear models. Within-MS continuous age regression and exploratory age-stratified ANOVA were evaluated with the same family definitions. Aperiodic offset showed the strongest diagnosis association under the specified age-adjusted model. However, the MS and HC age ranges did not overlap (21-55 vs 56-83 years), so the diagnosis coefficient depends on extrapolation and cannot establish an MS-specific effect. papers.title: Theta-band EEG changes following sequential rTMS and tACS in fibromyalgia: A randomized controlled pilot study

Methods: In this exploratory randomized controlled pilot study, 10 adults with fibromyalgia were assigned to active stimulation (n = 5) or a no-stimulation control group (n = 5). Active participants received one or two sessions of 10-Hz rTMS over the left primary motor cortex (1,000 pulses/session), followed by 10 daily sessions of bilateral 10-Hz tACS (1 mA, 20 min). Six-minute eyes-closed resting-state EEG recordings were obtained before and after the intervention or an equivalent control interval. Power spectral density was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands and analyzed using mixed repeated-measures ANOVAs across central-centroparietal and posterior regions of interest. Results: Theta power increased significantly in the active group but not in controls, yielding significant Time x Group (F(1,8)=8.70, p=.018, p2=.521) and Time x ROI x Group (F(1,8)=5.53, p=.047, p2=.409) interactions. Follow-up analyses showed increased theta power in both central-centroparietal (p=.004) and posterior (p=.012) regions, with a larger increase observed posteriorly. No significant interaction effects were found for delta, alpha, or beta power. Conclusions: Sequential motor-cortex rTMS followed by repeated bilateral 10-Hz tACS was associated with increased resting-state theta activity in fibromyalgia. Given the small sample size, post hoc ROI selection, lack of sham stimulation, and absence of component-specific control conditions, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication in adequately powered sham-controlled studies.

papers.title: Ozone as a Catalyst for Alzheimer's Disease and Sleep Disorders: Implications for Neurodegeneration Induced by Air Pollution.
papers.abstract: Tropospheric ozone, a highly reactive air pollutant, has emerged as a potential environmental risk factor for Alzheimer's disease (AD) and its associated sleep disturbances, yet a comprehensive synthesis of the underlying mechanisms has remained limited. This narrative review summarizes experimental and epidemiological evidence on ozone exposure, neurodegeneration and disrupted sleep, organized around one working hypothesis: ozone generates a systemic oxidative-inflammatory signal that reaches the central nervous system, with sleep/circadian disruption and AD-related pathology as downstream outcomes that may reinforce each other. In experimental models, ozone is associated with oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, blood-brain barrier disruption, glial activation and neuroinflammation, overlapping with β-amyloid accumulation and tau hyperphosphorylation, and with reduced REM sleep and altered neurotransmitters; clock-gene changes have been shown mainly in peripheral tissue. Circadian disruption is a candidate effector, and current data cannot distinguish mediation from co-occurrence. Epidemiological evidence for ozone-specific associations with cognitive decline remains inconsistent at the population level compared with other pollutants such as PM2.5 or NO2, although some cohorts report pollutant-specific effects and modulation by the apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE4) genotype. Most experimental studies use concentrations well above regulatory ambient standards. Overall, ambient ozone is a biologically plausible, but not yet epidemiologically confirmed, candidate risk factor for AD and sleep disorders. Future work should prioritize exposure-graded longitudinal studies and clarification of the dose-response relationship, including the effects of controlled medical ozone.

papers.title: Oxidative Stress in Pediatric Obstructive Sleep Apnea Syndrome: A Narrative Review.
papers.abstract: Pediatric obstructive sleep apnea syndrome (OSAS) is a common sleep-related breathing disorder increasingly recognized as a multisystem disease rather than an isolated disorder of the upper airway. Recurrent episodes of upper airway obstruction generate intermittent hypoxia, reoxygenation, and sleep fragmentation, promoting excessive production of reactive oxygen and nitrogen species and disruption of antioxidant defenses. This narrative review summarizes current evidence regarding the mechanisms, biomarkers, and clinical consequences of oxidative stress in pediatric OSAS. Intermittent hypoxia activates several redox-sensitive pathways, including NADPH oxidases, hypoxia-inducible factor-1α, nuclear factor-κB, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endoplasmic reticulum stress, thereby creating a bidirectional relationship between oxidative stress and systemic inflammation. Pediatric studies have demonstrated alterations in lipid peroxidation products, glutathione redox balance, urinary 8-hydroxy-2'-deoxyguanosine, isoprostanes, NOX2-related markers, and inflammatory mediators. These abnormalities are associated with endothelial dysfunction and cardiovascular, neurocognitive, metabolic, hepatic, renal, and immune consequences, and several may improve following effective treatment. Importantly, the magnitude of oxidative and end-organ injury does not consistently parallel the apnea-hypopnea index, suggesting that hypoxic burden, obesity, genetic susceptibility, antioxidant capacity, and disease duration influence individual biological vulnerability. Although several oxidative biomarkers show potential for disease characterization and treatment monitoring, methodological heterogeneity and the absence of standardized pediatric reference values currently limit their clinical application. Future integration of polysomnographic hypoxic-burden metrics with oxidative, inflammatory, metabolomic, and genomic biomarkers may improve risk stratification and facilitate more personalized management of pediatric OSAS.

papers.title: Overt and Covert Speech-State Classification from Tripolar Concentric Ring Electrode EEG: A 4 mm and 10 mm Configuration Study.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) speech-state classification is a noninvasive method to identify the brain's overt and covert behavior. The EEG achieved through the scalp is contaminated by artifacts and volume conduction and suffers from poor spatial resolution. We present the first application of small 4 mm tripolar concentric ring electrodes (TCREs) to record the overt and covert EEG signals. In addition, EEG signals were recorded for overt and covert behavior using a 10 mm TCRE as a reference. Data were recorded from 16 participants (4 mm, n=8; 10 mm, n=8). Each participant completed 200 picture-naming trials (100 overt and 100 covert). The analysis includes task-to-baseline root mean square ratios, power spectral density, time frequency representation analysis and participant-wise overt and covert classification using linear discriminant analysis, support vector machines, and EEGNet. The overt speech produced higher task-to-baseline ratios than covert speech. In addition, EEGNet achieved the highest mean accuracy (84.06±15.57%), followed by SVM (81.56±14.23%) and LDA (76.56±15.30%).

papers.title: Total polyphenols from Hemerocallis citrina Baroni leaves improve sleep quality in mice with perimenopausal insomnia and are associated with altered expression of 5-HT1AR, ADCY5, PKA, and GABRA2.
papers.abstract: Hemerocallis citrina Baroni has a long history of dietary and medicinal use in China. Its dried whole herb is documented as an ethnic medicinal material in the 2003 edition of the Guizhou Provincial Quality Standards for Chinese Medicinal and Ethnic Medicinal Materials, while Hemerocallis flowers are traditionally used for "ye shao an mei" (), referring to reduced or disturbed sleep at night. Modern studies have demonstrated sleep-improving effects of the flowers, and previous work showed neuroprotective and antidepressant-like activities of total polyphenols from Hemerocallis citrina Baroni leaves (HLTP). However, the effects of HLTP on perimenopausal insomnia (PMI) remain unclear. To evaluate the effects of HLTP on sleep disturbances in mice exhibiting perimenopausal and insomnia-like features and investigate associated molecular changes. HLTP was prepared using a previously reported procedure. Network pharmacology predicted candidate targets and pathways for 32 phenolic constituents identified in an earlier HLTP batch, while molecular docking assessed predicted binding to 10 core targets selected by protein-protein interaction (PPI) analysis. A composite mouse model was generated using 4-vinylcyclohexene dioxide (VCD) to induce perimenopausal features, followed by para-chloro-DL-phenylalanine (PCPA) to induce insomnia-like disturbances. Seventy female C57BL/6J mice were randomized into seven groups (n = 10 per group): Control, Con+HLTP, Model, HLTP-L/M/H (10, 20, and 40 mg/kg, respectively), and zopiclone. Treatment began with model induction. Behavioral tests, pentobarbital-induced sleep testing, 24 h electroencephalographic/electromyographic (EEG/EMG) polysomnography, histopathology, biochemical assays, and Western blotting were used to evaluate pharmacological effects and associated molecular changes. 16S rRNA sequencing, serum untargeted metabolomics, and brain transcriptomics were additionally performed to characterize complementary changes in the gut microbiota, systemic metabolism, and central gene expression. Network pharmacology prioritized the serotonergic synapse pathway for further investigation. HLTP improved behavioral and sleep-related abnormalities, with the most consistent effects at the high dose. EEG/EMG polysomnography showed a partial shift in sleep-wake distribution toward the Control pattern. During the inactive phase, high-dose HLTP shortened non-rapid eye movement (NREM) and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep latencies, reduced Wake bout number and NREM-to-Wake transitions, prolonged NREM bout duration, and increased NREM sleep time (P < 0.05). HLTP also attenuated neuronal morphological abnormalities and improved sex hormone, monoamine neurotransmitter, oxidative stress, and inflammatory indicators. Western blotting showed increased expression of the 5-hydroxytryptamine 1A receptor (5-HT1AR) and gamma-aminobutyric acid type A receptor α2 subunit (GABRA2), together with decreased expression of adenylyl cyclase 5 (ADCY5) and protein kinase A (PKA) after HLTP treatment. Multi-omics analyses revealed changes in gut microbial composition, serum metabolism, and brain gene expression following HLTP treatment. Pathway enrichment analysis of exploratory candidate metabolites identified FDR-supported enrichment of steroid biosynthesis. Brain transcriptomics identified FDR-supported enrichment of circadian rhythm in the Model vs. Control comparison and neuroactive ligand-receptor interaction in the HLTP-H vs. Model comparison. None of the tested cross-omics correlations remained significant after FDR correction. HLTP ameliorated sleep disturbances in mice subjected to the VCD+PCPA composite model, accompanied by improvements in neuroendocrine indicators and changes in 5-HT1AR, ADCY5, PKA, and GABRA2 protein expression. The omics findings provided complementary exploratory evidence, although the functional relationships among these changes remain to be established.

papers.title: Strategies to establish a biologically defined Parkinson's disease cohort prior to the onset of clinically significant motor symptoms
papers.abstract: Identifying individuals at risk for neurodegeneration is a priority for clinical trials. Parkinson's Precision Medicine Initiative (PPMI) deploys strategies to enroll individuals before typical clinical Parkinson's disease symptoms: recruiting polysomnogram-confirmed REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) and central identification of hyposmia via smell testing. Groups were divided into RBD with and without hyposmia (RBD+Hyposmia, RBD-Hyposmia) and hyposmia with and without self-reported dream enactment behavior (Hyposmia+DEB, Hyposmia-DEB). Participants underwent clinical and biomarker testing including CSF alpha-synuclein seed amplification assay (CSFaSynSAA) and dopamine transporter imaging. While all enrollment strategies showed robust enrichment for CSFaSynSAA positivity, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia+DEB were more likely CSFaSynSAA+ (94% and 85%) vs RBD-Hyposmia (40%) and Hyposmia-DEB (55%). Among CSFaSynSAA+, RBD+Hyposmia and Hyposmia+DEB had more mood, autonomic, and cognitive symptoms than Hyposmia-DEB. PPMI identified a large biologically-defined early neuronal synucleinopathy cohort and demonstrated biomarker and multi-domain clinical heterogeneity within CSFaSynSAA+ individuals prior to symptom onset.

papers.title: Molecular mechanisms of YZG-331 ameliorated insomnia based on the gut microbiota-drug interaction.
papers.abstract: The gut microbiota plays a crucial role in the study of drug efficacy and metabolism. YZG-331 exhibits significant sedative and hypnotic effects. However, the oral bioavailability of YZG-331 in female mice remains low at 27.7%, and it exhibits instability in the gut microbiota, undergoing rapid metabolism, with the intestinal hydrolytic metabolite M2 identified as the characteristic metabolite. Both the underlying mechanisms of YZG-331 therapeutic effects on insomnia and its enzyme-mediated metabolic pathways involving the gut microbiota remain incompletely elucidated. In this study, we found that YZG-331 regulated the tryptophan metabolism and 5-HT production pathways by the gut microbiota. Specifically, YZG-331 increased the abundance of Lactobacillus and Muribaculaceae in the gut, with Lactobacillus reuteri playing a critical role in both the metabolic processes of YZG-331 and the biosynthesis of tryptophan-derived metabolites. YZG-331 enhanced the activation of the tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4) cofactor system, which subsequently promoted tryptophan hydroxylase (TPH) activity, thereby enhancing 5-HT production. Furthermore, YZG-331 and M2 increased intestinal butyric acid levels, thereby promoting sleep regulation and supporting the restoration of the intestinal barrier. Overall, our study provided the first evidence highlighting the crucial role of the gut microbiota in the therapeutic mechanism and metabolic processing of YZG-331 in the treatment of insomnia.

papers.title: Sleep Disturbances and Circadian Phase Delay in People Living with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV): A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: Advances in HIV research and antiretroviral therapy (ART) have substantially increased life expectancy among people living with HIV (PLHIV). However, challenges affecting quality of life and alterations in daily physiological processes persist. Among the health dimensions most affected are sleep quality and circadian rhythms, resulting in significant biological alterations. The main objective of this study is to analyze the existing scientific evidence regarding the effects of HIV on sleep quality and on the alignment and synchronization of circadian rhythms. The bidirectional interaction between these physiological alterations and associated clinical, immunological, and metabolic factors in people living with HIV (PLHIV) was evaluated, emphasizing their integration. For this review, searches were conducted in the PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science databases. Eligibility criteria were applied, resulting in a final selection of 15 studies based on search strategies. The findings demonstrated a high prevalence of poor sleep quality as well as delayed circadian phase. These chronobiological alterations were closely associated with systemic inflammation, altered melatonin levels, impaired cognitive performance, and an altered metabolic profile involving leptin, ghrelin, adiponectin, and peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor (PPAR) signaling. Despite the consistency of the results, the methodologies of individual studies varied, and a notable absence of clinical trials aimed at addressing poor sleep quality and chronodisruption was observed. A promising clinical approach involves complementing antiretroviral therapy (ART) with chronotherapeutic interventions and sleep hygiene. In conclusion, HIV can disrupt personal temporal organization at a systemic level; consequently, incorporating assessments of sleep and circadian rhythms into clinical care may be warranted, while chronotherapeutic interventions should be further investigated.

papers.title: Menopausal Symptom Burden and Self-Reported Poor Sleep Quality Among Japanese Working Women Aged 40 Years and Older: An Exploratory Cross-Sectional Study.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Sleep-related complaints are common among women in midlife and may reflect not only insufficient sleep duration but also broader menopausal symptom burden. Although menopausal symptoms and sleep problems are known to be related, less is known about how menopausal symptom domains are associated with self-reported sleep quality among working women, particularly when objective sleep duration is considered. This exploratory cross-sectional study aimed to examine the association between menopausal symptom burden and self-reported poor sleep quality among Japanese working women aged 40 years and older, while accounting for objectively measured sleep duration. Materials and Methods: Participants completed questionnaires on sleep quality and menopausal symptoms and underwent objective sleep monitoring using a wearable electroencephalography device. Self-reported sleep quality was assessed using an item corresponding to the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index and dichotomized into poor and good sleep quality. Menopausal symptoms were evaluated using the Simplified Menopausal Index, including vasomotor, psychological, and somatic domains, with higher scores indicating greater symptom burden. Results: Among 79 participants, 43 reported poor sleep quality and 36 reported good sleep quality. Women with poor sleep quality had higher total and domain-specific SMI scores and shorter objective sleep duration. In logistic regression analyses adjusted for age and objective sleep duration, total SMI score and each symptom domain were associated with poor sleep quality. These associations remained significant in sensitivity analyses excluding the sleep-related SMI item from the total score and psychological domain score. Conclusions: Self-reported poor sleep quality among Japanese working women aged 40 years and older may reflect menopausal symptom burden beyond objectively measured sleep duration. The consistency of the findings across sensitivity analyses supports the robustness of this association. Sleep complaints may therefore serve as an accessible signal for recognizing menopausal symptom burden in clinical and occupational health settings.

papers.title: Exploratory Metabolomic and Metagenomic Profiling of Fecal Samples in Isolated REM Sleep Behavior Disorder.
papers.abstract: Isolated REM sleep behavior disorder (iRBD) is among the most reliable prodromal markers of α-synucleinopathies. Under the body-first (gut-first) model of α-synuclein pathology, in which pathology may originate in the enteric nervous system and ascend to the brain, the gut is a biologically plausible compartment in which early and accessible molecular alterations might be detectable; however, the fecal metabolome remains poorly investigated in this population. In this exploratory, cross-sectional study of 21 iRBD patients and 15 healthy controls, we characterized fecal samples through an integrated multi-omics framework. The fecal metabolome was profiled on two complementary mass spectrometry platforms: HS-SPME GC-EI-high-resolution MS, used for both untargeted volatilomics and targeted quantification of linear and branched short-chain fatty acids, and untargeted LC-MS/MS for the non-volatile fraction. Gut microbial community composition was characterized on the same material by 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and the metabolomic and microbial layers were combined by DIABLO multi-omics integration. Linear short-chain fatty acids were preserved, whereas branched-chain fatty acids were selectively increased in iRBD, indicating a shift toward proteolytic fermentation. Volatile indole was reduced, while p-cresol and 2-octanone were increased, paralleled at the LC-MS/MS level by attenuation of the tryptophan-indole axis, class-level bile acid depletion, and increased acylcarnitines. The microbiome was depleted of Blautia and Faecalibacterium and enriched in Oscillospirales. Integration resolved a coherent host-microbe signature that discriminated iRBD patients from controls within this discovery cohort (84.8% cross-validated accuracy). These cross-sectional findings characterize candidate fecal signatures associated with iRBD; given the exploratory design and the limited sample size, they are hypothesis-generating, and their value for predicting phenoconversion remains to be established in prospective studies.

papers.title: Sleep quality, circadian rhythm disruption, functioning, and treatment adherence in major depression: a cross-sectional exploratory study.
papers.abstract: Sleep disturbances and circadian rhythm disruption are highly prevalent in major depressive disorder (MDD) and may contribute to poorer functioning and reduced treatment adherence. However, few studies have examined sleep quality, biological rhythm disruption, functioning, and medication adherence concurrently in an outpatient depression sample. This study investigated the relationships among sleep quality, biological rhythm, functional status, medication adherence, and depression severity in patients diagnosed with depression. A descriptive, correlational cross-sectional study was conducted in the Adult Psychiatry Outpatient Clinic of Maltepe University Faculty of Medicine Hospital between 16 December 2024 and 15 March 2025. A total of 110 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of depression were included. Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), biological rhythm disruption using the Biological Rhythm Interview of Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (BRIAN), functional status using the Social Functioning Scale (SFS-T), medication adherence using the Medication Adherence Rating Scale (MARS), and depression severity using the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI). Pearson correlation analyses were used to examine associations among variables, and multiple linear regression analyses were conducted to identify independent factors associated with sleep quality. Sleep impairment was common: 46.4% of participants reported moderate sleep quality and 31.8% reported poor sleep quality. Mean PSQI score was 8.31 (SD = 4.21). Poorer sleep quality (higher PSQI scores) was moderately associated with lower social functioning (r = - 0.300, p < 0.01) and lower medication adherence (r = - 0.350, p < 0.01), and strongly associated with greater biological rhythm disruption (r = 0.621, p < 0.01). Sleep quality was also positively correlated with depression severity (r = 0.494, p < 0.01). Sleep impairment was common: 46.4% of participants reported moderate sleep quality and 31.8% reported poor sleep quality. Poorer sleep quality (higher PSQI scores) was moderately associated with lower social functioning (r = - 0.300, p < 0.01) and lower medication adherence (r = - 0.350, p < 0.01), and positively associated with biological rhythm disruption (r = 0.621, p < 0.01) and depressive symptom severity (r = 0.494, p < 0.01). In this outpatient depression sample, poor sleep quality was significantly associated with circadian rhythm disruption, reduced functioning, lower medication adherence, and greater depressive symptom severity. These findings support the clinical value of early sleep screening and integrated approaches that address sleep-circadian regulation alongside functional recovery, with possible benefits for treatment engagement in outpatient mental health care. papers.title: Seasonal Variation, Circadian Patterns, and Night Eating Syndrome Among Older Adults: The Mediating Role of Sleep Quality.
papers.abstract: Objective: We aimed to examine whether sleep quality mediates the relationship between seasonal variation, circadian pattern, and night eating syndrome in community-dwelling older adults. Methods: A cross-sectional study was conducted with 336 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥ 60 years) recruited from geriatric social clubs. Participants completed validated instruments, including the Global Seasonality Scale (GSS), Morningness-Eveningness Questionnaire (MEQ), Night Eating Diagnostic Questionnaire (NEDQ), and Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI). Path analysis with bootstrapping (5000 resamples) was used to estimate direct and indirect associations among the study variables. Results: The mean age was 66.8 ± 5.9 years (56.8% male). Moderate to severe seasonal variation was observed in 68.2% of participants, while 85.1% reported poor sleep quality. Morning circadian pattern predominated (56.9%), and 23.2% met criteria for full night eating syndrome. Path analysis identified a significant indirect association between seasonal variation and circadian pattern through sleep quality (B = -0.038, 95% CI [-0.051, -0.026]), corresponding to 41% of the total modeled association. Similarly, a significant indirect association between seasonal variation and night eating syndrome through sleep quality was observed (B = 0.053, 95% CI [0.037, 0.068]), corresponding to 37% of the total modeled association. All direct and indirect paths were statistically significant (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Sleep quality was significantly involved in the observed relationships between seasonal variation, circadian pattern, and night eating syndrome among older adults, with the path models indicating both direct and indirect associations. These findings emphasize the interconnected nature of seasonal sensitivity, sleep characteristics, circadian preference, and nighttime eating behavior in later life. Further longitudinal research with repeated seasonal assessments is warranted to clarify the temporal relationships among these factors and to determine the potential value of sleep-focused preventive and clinical approaches.
